narrative:
The model has analyzed your academic journey and determined that there’s a **20% chance** you might not pass your final year. While this isn’t a certainty, it’s high enough that your school has decided you should take extra courses to help you succeed. Think of it like a warning sign on a road—it’s not saying you’ll definitely fail, but it’s telling you to slow down and take precautions.

The biggest reason behind this recommendation is your **study habits**. Compared to most students who aren’t at risk, you’re spending **less time studying each week**—only about 2 to 5 hours, while many successful students study 5 to 10 hours. This is the strongest factor pushing the model toward this concern. Even though you haven’t failed any classes before, the model sees that your current study routine might not be enough to handle the demands of your final year.

Another key factor is your **goals for the future**. You’ve said you want to pursue higher education, which is great! But the model notices that students who are *most* focused on long-term success often put in extra effort now. Since your study time is lower than average for students with similar ambitions, the model is gently nudging you to step up.

Finally, while you’re doing well in many areas—like having a supportive family and good relationships at home—your **number of school absences** (six so far) is higher than the average student who’s on track. Missing classes, even a few times, can make it harder to keep up, especially in your final year.

This doesn’t mean you’re failing now—it means the model is giving you a chance to adjust before it’s too late. The remedial courses are there to help you build stronger study habits, catch up on any gaps, and give you the support you need. The best thing you can do next is **take this seriously**: use the extra courses to refine your study routine, ask for help when needed, and make sure you’re giving your final year the focus it deserves. You’ve got this!
